expected_utility: Use the Expected Utility card to see how uncertainty becomes one comparable number before the state is known. The Bayes Rule card shows the companion move: once evidence arrives, the weights on those possible states must change.
extensive_form_games: The Backward Induction card explains why a game tree is more than a picture. Once choices happen over time, each earlier branch gets its meaning from the continuation choices that later players will actually want to make.
dominance: The Dominance Inequality card is the exact test behind the lecture's pruning move. It shows why one bad-looking row is not enough; the worse strategy must lose across every opponent action the model allows.
iterated_deletion: The Dominance Inequality card gives the one-round deletion test. Iterated deletion repeats that same comparison after the game has shrunk, which is why a locally simple inequality can generate a chain of reasoning.
rationalizability: The Expected Utility and Bayes Rule cards explain why rationalizability is not just guessing what others might do. A strategy survives only if it can be justified by some coherent belief about others' possible choices.
best_response: The Best Response card is the local engine of this concept. It turns the vague phrase 'my smartest move' into a conditional comparison: hold the rest fixed, evaluate my actions, and keep the payoff-maximizers.
nash_equilibrium: The Nash card closes the best-response loop, while the Best Response card shows the one-player test inside it. Together they explain why equilibrium is mutual consistency rather than social optimality.
mixed_strategies: The Nash and Expected Utility cards explain why randomization is not noise. A player may mix only when the expected payoffs make several actions equally defensible against the opponent's own strategic uncertainty.
zero_sum_games: The Nash and Best Response cards show the two sides of zero-sum reasoning: each player is locally responding, but the payoff map makes one player's gain exactly the other player's loss.
minimax: The Best Response card gives the local comparison that minimax hardens into a worst-case rule. Instead of asking what outcome is likely, the player asks which action protects them against the opponent's most damaging response.
backward_induction: The Backward Induction card is the procedure behind this concept. It shows how the course converts future choice points into present values, then uses those values to decide what earlier action is credible.
subgame_perfection: The Backward Induction card explains the credibility test inside subgame perfection, and the Nash card explains the equilibrium requirement. The concept combines them: every later subgame must pass its own no-deviation check.
one_shot_deviation: The Backward Induction card shows why one local deviation can reveal a broken sequential plan. If a player would switch at a future node, the earlier strategy profile was never fully credible.
bargaining: The Discounted Payoff Sum card explains why time itself changes bargaining power. Waiting is not free: future surplus is converted into present value, so delay can make a formally larger future payoff less attractive.
finitely_repeated_games: The Backward Induction card explains the unraveling logic in finite repetition. Once the final period has no future discipline, that answer changes the previous period, and the reasoning walks backward.
infinitely_repeated_games: The Discounted Payoff Sum card is the mathematical pressure behind repeated cooperation. The question is whether the present value of future punishment is large enough to outweigh the one-period temptation to defect.
folk_theorem: The Discounted Payoff Sum card explains how patience can support many outcomes, while the Nash card supplies the no-deviation test. The folk theorem lives where future discipline can make today's restraint privately worthwhile.
implicit_cartels: The Discounted Payoff Sum card explains why a cartel can survive without a written contract: future lost profits can discipline today's undercutting. The auction payment card appears when market rules also shape strategic payments.
imperfect_competition: The Best Response card shows why firms cannot choose price or quantity in isolation. Each firm's move is evaluated against rivals' moves, so market outcomes come from intersecting response incentives.
bayesian_games: The Expected Utility card shows how a player chooses before knowing the hidden type, and the Bayes Rule card shows how beliefs should move when information arrives. Bayesian games need both pieces.
types_and_beliefs: The Bayes Rule card explains how observations revise type probabilities, while Expected Utility explains how those probabilities guide choice before the type is known. The concept is the bridge between hidden facts and action.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium: Expected Utility gives the payoff comparison under hidden information, Best Response gives the conditional choice test, and Nash Equilibrium closes the loop across types. The result is equilibrium with uncertainty kept inside the model.
screening_and_adverse_selection: Bayes Rule explains how observed choices reveal hidden types, Expected Utility explains choice before revelation, and the auction payment card shows the related design problem: rules must make private information strategically visible.
auctions: The Auction Expected Payment card separates the bid, the chance of winning, and the payment if winning. Expected Utility and Bayes Rule explain why bidders must reason over rival values they cannot directly see.
revenue_equivalence: The Auction Expected Payment card is the useful entry point because revenue equivalence is not about identical rules. It asks when different auction formats create the same expected payment pattern under the same underlying environment.
ad_auctions: The Auction Expected Payment card explains why platform auctions are not just rank lists. A bid changes both allocation chances and payments, so incentives depend on the expected payment rule created by the mechanism.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium: Bayes Rule explains belief updating after observed play, Backward Induction explains sequential credibility, and Expected Utility explains optimal choice under those beliefs. PBE needs all three to keep dynamic information games disciplined.
signaling: Bayes Rule explains how a receiver reads a signal as evidence about hidden type, while Expected Utility and payment-style incentive reasoning explain why the sender may or may not find that signal worth choosing.
cheap_talk: Bayes Rule explains how messages can change beliefs, but the Expected Utility and incentive cards show the danger: because messages are cheap, communication works only when sender incentives make the words credible.
common_knowledge: The Common Knowledge Recursion card shows why coordination can require more than everyone knowing the same fact. The strategic force comes from the repeated public chain: I know, I know you know, and so on.
